1: The argument says advertising only raises prices and harms consumers. B gives a benefit: competition through advertising improves quality.
2:
Law controls few people; communities control most through social attitudes; mass unemployment creates people who reject those attitudes 'and hence' subverts society. The main conclusion: large-scale unemployment subverts society — A.
E and C are steps towards it; B is a premise; D isn't stated.
3: The passage says sentimental marketing would be attacked from others, yet John Lewis outperforms all rivals with it. So an appeal to sentiment can succeed in the right hands — E.
4:
Drink, drugs, prison and suicide figures are all shifting from young to middle-aged people. So some social problems are increasingly those of the middle-aged — B.
A, C, D and E go beyond the evidence.
5: The argument finds evidence that fits the theory and concludes it is true. Confirming evidence supports a theory but doesn't prove it — D.
6: The argument says speed reading is of limited use to students who need deep understanding. C weakens it: a student finds reading quickly improves understanding.
7: The argument concludes that carrying a gun makes you more likely to be shot. C reverses the cause: people already at risk are more likely to carry guns.
8: The argument says more three-way meetings will help exam results by revealing problems. That assumes the meetings work — the three parties can exchange views constructively — B.
9: More rice-takers reported arousal than horn-takers, and the argument concludes horn isn't an aphrodisiac. Using rice as the comparison assumes rice itself has no real aphrodisiac effect — A.
10: The argument: information now can't be censored or removed, so governments and media must adapt. C adds that posting anonymously avoids prosecution, making control even harder.
11: The argument says laptops are of limited use once their battery runs out, so they shouldn't be allowed. But owners could still use them until then (and for other things) — E.
12: Premises: shorter degrees mean lower-quality graduates; universities should resist anything that lowers graduate quality. Conclusion: universities should oppose two-year degrees — B.
13:
Celebrities' behaviour will be imitated, so their refusal to be role models is 'unrealistic and irresponsible'. The conclusion: they should act responsibly because they are role models whether they like it or not — B.
E contradicts the passage.
14: The argument assumes an alarm makes a house less likely to be burgled. C undermines that: burglars see alarms as a sign of valuables, so alarmed houses may be targeted more.
15: The writer says that if the work has emotional force and complexity, video can be great art. That assumes emotional force and complexity are enough for great art — A.
16: The Greeks are used as proof that people can stay moral without religious faith. C weakens it: many Greeks questioned whether being moral had any value.
17: The argument says rising house prices cause debt problems, so governments should stop prices rising above inflation. A supports it: prices keep pulling away from salaries, making the problem worse.
18: The argument concludes low budgets make popular films. It overlooks that cost may not be what makes a film popular — C.
19: The passage rejects the taunt: there's no hypocrisy in arguing for equality from a privileged position. So someone can be a genuine socialist with a high standard of living — B.
20: The evidence comes from simulator experiments, but the conclusion is about real roads. That assumes simulators reflect real driving — A.
21:
Unreported accidents and steady hospital admissions suggest the fall in recorded accidents may not be real. So optimism about road safety may be unfounded — A.
B and D are too strong; C and E aren't concluded.
22: The argument says results reflect politics, not music. C gives another explanation for bloc voting: neighbouring countries share musical tastes.
23: The argument goes from 'success is measured by possessions' to 'people with few possessions must feel a failure'. That assumes those people want to be seen as successful — E.
24: The proposal: only donors (or those who agree to donate) get transfusions. A weakens it: some people can't give blood, so the rule would be unfair and couldn't apply to everyone.
25:
Children without a set bedtime scored lower, especially at age three. So irregular bedtimes may disrupt cognitive development — B.
A goes beyond the evidence (bedtime hour didn't matter); C, D and E are too strong or off-topic.
26: The argument says private-school pupils must get higher grades. D gives another explanation for their numbers at Oxbridge: a larger share of them take A-levels at all.
27: The argument says compulsory insurance would mean insurers, not taxpayers, pay for injuries. That assumes all dog owners would obey the law and get insured — C.
28: Despite possible economic sense, 'the privatisation of prisons is nonetheless wrong' — the main conclusion (B). The points about State power, disturbed prisoners and private firms are reasons for it.
29:
The argument describes the advantages of burning willow and ends 'We should follow their example': we should use willow to generate electricity — B.
C, D and E are reasons; A is the starting point.
30: The recommendation is that schools teach the link between extremism and war to make war less likely. That assumes such teaching would make fewer people vote for extremists — C.
